title: FRM Foundations, Lesson 1: The Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework
subtitle: Three lines of defence, risk appetite and risk limits: why risk is not the risk department's private business
whyItMatters: Most large financial disasters happened not because nobody saw the risk, but because the governance structure contained no mechanism that forced anyone to act on it. ERM is the framework that answers: who is responsible for what, and which boundary may not be crossed even while the money is being made.
openingQuestion: In the three lines of defence model, who is the first line responsible for managing risk?
openingOptions: The company's independent Risk Management function
The business unit that directly creates the risk
explanation: The first line is the business itself (the trading desk, credit, operations) - they create the risk, so they have to be the first to control it day by day. The second line (Risk, Compliance) provides independent oversight. The third line (Internal Audit) assesses whether the first two are actually working.

diagram.label: Line 1: the business controls its own risk
Line 2: Risk & Compliance provide independent oversight
Line 3: Internal Audit assesses both lines above
The board sets risk appetite for the whole organisation

realWorldExample.description: Nick Leeson was both the trader and the person settling his own trades in Singapore - line 1 and part of line 2's job merged into one seat. Nobody independently checked his real positions for over two years. The loss hidden in account 88888 quietly swelled to £827 million, enough to erase a 233-year-old bank within weeks of being discovered.

quiz.question: How does risk appetite differ from a risk limit?
options: Risk limits apply only to credit risk, while risk appetite applies only to market risk exposure
The two are exactly the same concept; only the name differs from one bank to the next
Traders at each desk set the appetite themselves daily, while the board reviews limits once a year
Appetite is the high-level statement of acceptable risk; limits are the concrete numbers pushed down to each desk
quiz.explanation: Risk appetite is a board-level statement (for instance: we will not accept a loss of more than X% of capital in one year). A risk limit is a concrete number - a VaR limit, a stop-loss, a counterparty credit line - broken down to each desk so that the total risk stays inside the appetite that was set. Both concepts cover every risk type, and the direction of authority runs from the board downward, never from the desk upward.

quiz.question: Why does the three lines of defence model require line 2 to be independent of line 1 in its reporting?
options: So line 2 is not swayed by line 1's sales pressure when it flags a risk
Because banking law in every country requires exactly this structure
Because line 2 needs to run on different software from line 1
So that line 2 can be paid a bonus based on line 1's revenue growth
quiz.explanation: If the person controlling risk reports to the person creating it (or is rewarded on their trading results), the incentive tilts toward staying quiet when something is wrong. Independent reporting - usually straight to the CRO or the board - is the condition that lets line 2 say no. Paying line 2 on line 1's revenue is the exact failure the structure exists to prevent, and software choice has nothing to do with it.

quiz.question: In the Barings Bank collapse, what was the core governance failure?
options: The bank had no risk management function and no internal control process on paper at all
One individual both traded and settled, erasing the line between line 1 and oversight
The Japanese market moved so violently that nobody could possibly have foreseen it
The bank was hit by a cyberattack that exposed its trading positions
quiz.explanation: Leeson held both the trader role (placing orders) and the settlement role (confirming and reconciling them) - precisely the functions that must be split so that one checks the other. Merging them is a structural failure, not a market failure: the policies existed on paper, and the market move only revealed a hole that had been open for two years.

quiz.question: What is the board's role in an ERM framework?
options: Approving every single trade on every desk directly
Replacing the risk management function in the firm entirely
Setting risk appetite and overseeing compliance
Meeting only once a crisis has already broken out in full
quiz.explanation: The board works at the strategic layer: setting the level of risk acceptable for the whole organisation, approving the ERM framework, and reviewing regular risk reporting. Managing the risk of individual transactions belongs to lines 1 and 2. A board that approves trades has taken on line 1's job and lost its independence, and one that meets only in a crisis has abandoned oversight altogether.

quiz.question: Why must risk limits be cascaded down to individual units rather than set only at group level?
options: Because the group limit is only reviewed once a year
Because regulators require each business unit's limit to be disclosed
Because unit limits must always sum exactly to the group limit
Because whoever decides daily needs to know their own boundary
quiz.explanation: A high-level risk appetite is a statement of direction; it only bites once it becomes a number the trader can see on screen. Without the cascade, everyone interprets it differently and nobody knows the true aggregate. Unit limits usually sum to less than the group limit rather than exactly to it, precisely to leave headroom, and disclosure of internal limits is not a regulatory requirement.

keyTakeaways: Three lines of defence: line 1 (the business) controls its own risk, line 2 (Risk/Compliance) provides independent oversight, line 3 (Internal Audit) assesses both
Risk appetite is a board-level statement; a risk limit is the concrete number that turns that appetite into something each desk can see
Independent reporting between line 1 and line 2 is a precondition, not a formality
Merging the trading role and the control or settlement role in one person is the classic structural failure that leads to disaster (Barings, 1995)

practicePrompt.question: A securities firm lets the same employee both place buy and sell orders and reconcile the books at the end of the day for their own trades. What is the biggest risk here?
options: That employee is overloaded and their productivity falls
There is no independent control line left to catch it
The company must pay more for a combined-role position
Customers will complain about slow order processing
practicePrompt.explanation: This is precisely the structural failure of the Barings collapse: merging line 1 and the control function in one person removes the early detection mechanism. The problem is not efficiency or cost, it is that nobody independent is left to check.

summary.keyIdea: ERM is not a department but a three-tier structure of responsibility that guarantees somebody independent is always watching the risk
summary.commonMistake: Treating risk management as the Risk department's private business, when line 1 - the people creating the risk - is the first and most important line of control
summary.action: For any process you own, ask: who is line 1, who is the independent line 2, and are they genuinely separate in their reporting.

application.title: Draw the three lines for a process you know
application.message: Pick a process you are part of - expense approval, credit approval, order placement - and write real names into each line. Then test the hard condition: does line 2 report to someone other than the person line 1 reports to. If it is the same boss, line 2 is independent only on the org chart.
application.secondary: The most common breakage is one person both creating a transaction and confirming it. Look for anyone in your process who sits in both places.

sections.text: Most large financial collapses do not begin with a single insane decision, but with a series of small ones that nobody was responsible for stopping. ERM exists to answer one question: when risk crosses the line, who is obliged to speak up.

sections.title: Who is responsible for what
sections.subtitle: Each line answers a different question about the same risk

concepts.def: The business unit that directly creates the risk (trading, credit, operations) - responsible for managing it day by day inside the limits it has been given.
Risk Management and Compliance - independent oversight, setting policy, and checking whether line 1 is staying inside its limits.
Internal Audit - assessing whether both line 1 and line 2 actually work as designed, reporting straight to the board.

sections.label: Easily confused
sections.text: Risk appetite and risk limit are not the same thing. Appetite is a high-level statement of direction ('we will not accept a loss of more than 5% of capital in one year'). A limit is the concrete number applied to each desk to make that statement real - the FX desk's VaR limit, a counterparty credit line, a daily stop-loss.

When the first two lines collapse into one person - as they did with Nick Leeson at Barings - the system loses its ability to find its own errors before they take the whole bank down. This is not market risk but governance structure risk: it materialises even when markets are entirely normal.

lines: ERM is not compliance paperwork; it is the answer to the question of who is obliged to say no.
Next lesson: why even a correct governance structure can be silenced by the wrong risk culture.
